questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following:

(i) Vernalisation.

(ii) Photoperiodism. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Vernalisation** is the **promotion of flowering by exposing the seeds, seedlings or plants to a period of low temperature (about 0 to 10 $^\circ$C) for several weeks**. Without this cold treatment the plant stays vegetative or flowers late. It is found in **winter cereals (winter wheat, rye)** and **biennials**; it makes the plant flower in the right season (spring or summer) after winter.

**(ii) Photoperiodism** is the **response of a plant (or animal) to the relative lengths of day (light) and night (darkness) in a 24-hour period (the photoperiod)**, e.g. the control of **flowering**, leaf fall and dormancy by the length of the night.

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe the effects of photoperiods on plants. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Photoperiod controls flowering.** Plants are grouped according to the day length needed to flower:

- **Short-day plants (SDP)** flower when the **day is shorter than a critical length** (the night is longer than a critical length), e.g. chrysanthemum, soya bean, rice, tobacco (Maryland Mammoth).
- **Long-day plants (LDP)** flower when the **day is longer than a critical length**, e.g. spinach, lettuce, wheat, radish, Henbane.
- **Day-neutral plants (DNP)** flower whatever the day length, e.g. maize, cucumber, tomato, sunflower, cotton.

What counts is the **length of the uninterrupted dark period**: in a short-day plant, a **brief flash of light (red light) in the middle of the long night prevents flowering**, while in a long-day plant it promotes flowering. The light is detected by the pigment **phytochrome** (red light converts $P_r$ to $P_{fr}$, far-red light reverses it).

**Other effects of the photoperiod:** **leaf fall and bud dormancy** of deciduous trees in the short days of autumn, formation of **tubers** (potato, short days) and **bulbs** (onion, long days), and **vegetative growth** and runner formation.

questions.enonce_markdown:
How is the speed of impulse transmission along a nerve fibre affected by:

(i) diameter of the axon.

(ii) myelin sheath. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Diameter of the axon.** The **larger the diameter, the faster the impulse**. A wide axon has **less resistance to the flow of ions** (the local circuit currents) in the axoplasm, so the **depolarisation spreads farther ahead** of each active region and the next part of the membrane reaches the **threshold** sooner. *Example:* the giant axon of the squid (about 500 $\mu$m) conducts at about 25 m s$^{-1}$, whereas a thin unmyelinated fibre of a mammal (about 1 $\mu$m) conducts at only about 0.5 to 2 m s$^{-1}$.

**(ii) Myelin sheath.** Myelin is a **fatty layer made by Schwann cells** wrapped around the axon; it is an **electrical insulator** that stops ions from crossing the membrane. It has gaps, the **nodes of Ranvier**, about 1 mm apart, and **sodium and potassium channels are concentrated at the nodes**.

- In a **myelinated fibre** the action potential occurs **only at the nodes**: the local currents **jump from one node to the next (saltatory conduction)**, which is **much faster** (up to 100 m s$^{-1}$ or more) and uses **less energy**, since fewer ions have to be pumped back by the sodium-potassium pump.
- In an **unmyelinated fibre** the depolarisation must be regenerated **continuously along the whole length** of the membrane, which is **slow** (0.5 to 2 m s$^{-1}$).
- Loss of myelin (e.g. in **multiple sclerosis**) **slows or blocks** impulse conduction.

questions.enonce_markdown: Briefly describe the transmission of an impulse across the synapse. *[6 marks]* *(4, 3, 7, 6 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **synapse** is the junction between the **presynaptic neurone** (terminal knob) and the **postsynaptic neurone**, separated by the **synaptic cleft** (about 20 nm). Transmission is **chemical** (e.g. with the transmitter **acetylcholine**):

1. The **action potential arrives** at the presynaptic terminal and **depolarises** it.
2. **Voltage-gated calcium channels open** and **Ca$^{2+}$ ions enter** the terminal.
3. Ca$^{2+}$ makes the **synaptic vesicles** containing the neurotransmitter **move to the presynaptic membrane and fuse with it**, releasing the transmitter into the cleft by **exocytosis**.
4. The transmitter **diffuses across the cleft** and **binds to specific receptor proteins** on the **postsynaptic membrane**.
5. This opens **sodium channels (ligand-gated)**; **Na$^+$ ions enter** and the membrane is **depolarised** (an excitatory postsynaptic potential). If the **threshold** is reached, an **action potential** starts in the postsynaptic neurone.
6. The transmitter is then **removed**: **acetylcholinesterase breaks acetylcholine into choline and ethanoate (acetate)**, which are taken back into the presynaptic knob and **resynthesised** into acetylcholine using **ATP from the many mitochondria**. This stops the continuous stimulation of the postsynaptic neurone.

The synapse allows impulses to pass in **one direction only** (vesicles are only in the presynaptic knob) and causes a short **delay (about 0.5 ms)**.
